author: RosieCampbell
text: For all these reasons, I'm not sure if I'll end up going fully vegan, but I want to commit to it for January as a personal challenge and as an experiment to better understand the benefits and costs.

author: RosieCampbell
text: I also acknowledge that focusing attention on personal diet changes may be less effective than focusing on corporate campaigns and/or improving meat alternatives

author: RosieCampbell
text: I actually suspect that modeling a pragmatic, primarily plant-based approach that shows people they can reduce without giving things up entirely is potentially a higher-impact strategy at this point than going fully vegan.

author: RosieCampbell
text: I think it would be better for the animals and for the environment if lots of people significantly reduced their intake of animal products than if only a few people gave them up entirely while everyone else maintained their current habits.

author: RosieCampbell
text: But even though I think factory farming is terrible, I think there are significant costs (social, financial, time, mental health, and others) to going fully vegan, which are often under-appreciated by activists.

author: RosieCampbell
text: (this is related to bundle of broader moral intuitions I have around death and suffering which I'm yet to resolve - a thread for another time)

author: RosieCampbell
text: It's the suffering I have the main issue with; I'm not (currently) convinced that eating animal products is inherently morally wrong if they are treated well and killed painlessly

author: RosieCampbell
text: I think future humans will look back on factory farming as a moral catastrophe. Almost all meat, dairy, and eggs involve a huge amount of suffering (even ones marketed as humane)

author: RosieCampbell
text: If I was only concerned about health, I don't think it would be necessary to cut out eggs, low-fat dairy, lean meat, or fish. That's where the ethics component comes in.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Beyond that, people are so different it seems vastly different things can work for different people. I feel happiest and healthiest when I eat high-carb, low-fat, which is well-suited to a plant-based diet with lots of whole grains (but I know other people prefer the opposite!)

author: RosieCampbell
text: As fas as I can tell nutrition science is mostly a mess, but if there's anything we can be reasonably confident in it's "eat whole foods, mostly plants"

author: RosieCampbell
text: People cut out animal products for a variety of reasons, including health, ethics, and the environment. For me it's a mix of all three.

author: RosieCampbell
text: I'm going to do Veganuary https://t.co/3cZBhxkQgF (i.e., be vegan for January 2020). Some thoughts:

author: RosieCampbell
text: @matthias_code Yesss they are so good! The downside is I really struggle to sleep on normal pillows now - I ended up buying a travel size buckwheat one as well so I can bring it with me when I travel 😅

author: RosieCampbell
text: @cnorthwood I still don't trust myself enough to not use an alarm at all, so I set one just in case for the latest I can afford to wake up but usually find I wake up naturally before it goes off

author: RosieCampbell
text: I suspected my bedroom might be below the recommended humidity level, but decided to measure it before buying a humidifier. Turned out my room was in the normal range

author: RosieCampbell
text: I sleep better when I breath through my nose. I tried taping my mouth shut for a while to get into the habit. I also tried nasal spray and nose cones but didn't feel like these made much of a difference

author: RosieCampbell
text: I drink a load of water before bed and have a bottle of water next to me in case I wake up thirsty in the night

author: RosieCampbell
text: I bought fancy new cotton percale sheets which are much cooler and more comfortable (and a higher quality duvet)

author: RosieCampbell
text: Another strategy I sometimes use if my mind is racing is to make a deal with myself to spend 20 minutes worrying about The Thing in the morning (you can even block it out on your calendar so you trust you'll do it)

author: RosieCampbell
text: I use an eye mask, and have a kind of pavlovian response now such that as soon as I put it on my brain knows it's time to sleep. It has built in earphones which is handy for listening to podcasts when I need to distract my racing mind https://t.co/x3ilkGaW45

author: RosieCampbell
text: Caffeine doesn't seem to noticeably affect me, but I've mostly switched to decaf just in case (since I didn't get a buzz from caffeine anyway it's not a big deal to me either way)

author: RosieCampbell
text: Looking at screens before bed seems to have no negative effect on my sleep. I do use 'night light' settings to reduce blue light but can't tell if this makes much of a difference

author: RosieCampbell
text: I sleep better when I go to bed at the same time every night, but this isn't always possible, and am usually ok if I get to bed between 9pm and 11:30pm. I know my sleep will suffer if I don't get to bed before midnight - but sometimes that's a trade-off I accept

author: RosieCampbell
text: I've started sleeping with my blinds open, so that I wake up with the sun. This is a much gentler way to wake up than an alarm and it helps keep my wake up time relatively consistent.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Buckwheat pillows are way better than normal pillows, especially for side sleepers https://t.co/NWjkaxq4NK

author: RosieCampbell
text: Temperature is super important, and your bedroom should probably be colder than you think. I sleep much better now that I have an apartment where I can control the AC; 65-68°F is my preferred range (~18-20°C)

author: RosieCampbell
text: This year I prioritized improving my sleep. I'm pretty happy with the results: I used to be tired basically all the time and now I almost always get a decent night's sleep when I can control my environment. Here are some things I've learned:

author: RosieCampbell
text: Examples like this are why I'm worried about AI alignment and misspecified objectives: it's so easy to fall prey to Goodhart's Law and optimize for the target when it's not the thing you actually care about (even as humans who should know better!) (4/4)

author: RosieCampbell
text: You can immediately eliminate D because its year is the odd one out - all the others are in the 80s. Of the three that are left, you can see that B and C share a month and A and C share a year. A question designer likely starts with the correct answer and makes (2/4)

author: RosieCampbell
text:
Here's an example of how I used to game multiple choice questions:

When did de Klerk become president of South Africa? 
A. 8/89
B. 9/88
C. 9/89
D. 8/98

Without even reading the question, you can guess the answer from the configuration of options (try before reading on!) (1/4)
